conversations.title: Start with the city bike-share data. Compare weekday and weekend demand by hour, keep member and casual riders visible, and write the first figure and compact summary tables.
Now look at who rides and where the network is under pressure. Summarize members versus casual riders, rank stations by peak utilization, and make a heatmap for rebalancing.
Put the three answers in results/summary.md, with links to the figures and the assumptions behind this compact example.

skills.content:
Start with rho_index: select an owner or search, then rho_resolve only the operations
needed now. Use rho_call with the complete contractRef. The private connection supplies
the project; discovery never grants additional authority or starts a runtime.
Independent third-party plugins: extension.list shows installed packages, extension.describe
gives their digest, operations and Skill entries. Read extension.content (kind skill)
before extension.call. Keep expectedDigest and the original changeId for a native call;
extension.read observes pending or unknown outcomes without rerunning. Installation and
management belong to the local person; plugin code never expands this connection grant.
Large replies carry a result reference. Use rho_read to inspect its fields and fetch
only selected text ranges or array pages. Retain useful references; release finished
results explicitly. Never repeat an action just to retrieve a large reply.
Writes use their owner’s conditions and original identity. A lost acknowledgement
requires observing that request; unchanged work never receives a replacement ID.
Declare produced figures as media. resource.list or artifact.check returns their
registered references; bind those directly with composition.apply, including artifacts
inside owner state. Do not manually register internal paths. A layout acknowledgement
alone does not prove the browser displayed the result.
A runtime HTML plugin view joins the same Studio composition tree. After extension.describe,
place one view with component "rho.extension.html", version "1", bindings {}, and props
{ title, pluginId, expectedDigest, entryId }. Read composition.read first and use a conditional
composition.apply against its current version. The saved digest prevents an update from silently
changing the view; after an update, read extension.describe again and reopen it with the new digest.
People and Agents share the document buffer and conditional save operation.
When the person should see or change a run’s inputs before it starts, propose it
instead of submitting it: composition.apply a view with component "rho.action",
version "1", bindings {} and props {title, action, actionVersion, operationId, input}.
The input is the action’s full input. The person submits it once under that
operationId; observe it with action.lookup and never submit that operationId yourself.
A person reaches you by pasting a request Rho copied for them. It names a context
or a run: read it with context.read or action.lookup before acting. They may stop a
run or export it as files; a stopped run is not resubmitted under its own operationId.

A person opens a folder themselves; an Agent is not required to read it.

1. project.entries lists one level of a folder inside the project, bounded and
   confined to the folder it names, skipping owner state and symbolic links. Pass
   path to descend; ".." and absolute paths are refused. The project folder also
   lists the source folders it works in as @<sourceId> entries, and those descend
   the same way, so a project made from source folders is not an empty listing.
2. project.openFile opens one text file as a document and places a single editor
   view for it in the tab layout. Opening the same file again folds into one view.
3. A file the person opened is a document in the shared buffer: they and the Agent
   edit and conditionally save the same text.

The boundary is deliberate and worth stating to a person who asks: a tab may read
its folder, edit a buffer and conditionally save it; it may not register resources, run
anything or reach a sibling project. Those stay Agent or operator work. When a
person expects otherwise, say which rule refuses them rather than reporting a bug.

Files the project shows as registered are not the same as files in the folder: the
sidebar counts registered resources, while the Overview lists the folder itself.

skills.content:
Describe the whole task yourself: Rho fixes no closed list of kinds or states.

1. task.map.declare carries stable item IDs, your own kind and state words (each a
   label, an optional tone and an optional role Rho understands: working, waiting,
   done, planned, unknown, stopped), titles you write, progress counted from real
   receipts, an optional layout view per item, and next only for steps you will take.
2. task.map.present changes a card form, its parameters (a subset), or the focus.
   People use the same call. A pinned target, or a change within agentFormIntervalMs
   of your last applied form change, is merged into one pending suggestion instead of
   being applied: the screen stays steady and the person applies it.
3. task.map.respond is the person only: pin, unpin, revert your form change (layout
   only, never the work), accept or dismiss a suggestion.
4. task.map.read observes. Reading never starts, resumes or reruns work.
5. Declare the map when you start, not when you are done, and declare again as the
   work moves: until then the person sees your calls but not their structure.
6. Name what an item rests on. As soon as artifact.check verifies a result, give the
   item artifact {id, version}; use from for an item that branches from another. Rho
   links an item to objects only through these references, never through its title.
7. Mark a line judgment: true when it is your reading of a result rather than
   something a record shows. It is shown as your judgment, never as verified.

A form declared zoom: false is reached only by naming it, so stepping up from a card
lands on the summary, not on compare.

skills.content:
A whole analysis has to survive interruption. Rho keeps no step cap and no wall time
by default, and a long analysis may still be stopped by the person or by the Agent
client, so write results as you go instead of holding them until the end.

1. Spend calls on the analysis, not on discovery. Resolve the operations you will use
   once each (kernel.run, kernel.read, kernel.interrupt, resource.list) and reuse the
   contractRef you were given. In the runs behind this Skill one Agent spent 36
   capability.index calls in a single analysis and ended with only its quality-control
   table written.
2. Do not guess what a result reference contains. A refused read means the shape is
   wrong, not that the result is missing: resolve the operation that produced it and
   read the page or range it names instead of trying sibling paths.
3. Nothing wakes you later. No monitor, timer or event resumes your turn: a cell still
   running when you stop is left running for nobody, and ending your reply is not
   proof the analysis finished. Pass a waitMs long enough for the slowest step (a
   normalisation over 90,000 nuclei can take many minutes), or read the cell with
   kernel.read in your own next call.
4. Load once, build on it. A session keeps what a cell defines, so read the data in one
   cell and derive in the next. A service restart does not keep those objects: the code
   and its outputs stay, the values in memory do not, so keep a script that rebuilds
   what matters.
5. Prefer a few large cells to many small ones, and keep each short enough to finish. A
   cell that hangs costs time: interrupt it with kernel.interrupt and continue with the
   part that is cheap to redo.
6. Draw to an explicit device. In these runs a ggsave call in the shared session hung
   and the figure had to be redrawn with png() and dev.off(): open the device, plot,
   close it, and let the figure land in a file you name.
7. Write each file once, complete, and save it to disk before you rely on it. One script
   written in full and then run costs less than the same script edited piece by piece,
   and a file on disk is the only version that outlives a stop. Run it in the session
   with kernel.run (source() in R, exec() in Python), not from a shell: a figure file
   stays readable mark by mark only while it holds the bytes a Notebook cell saved.
8. Check packages in one call, and do not install into a temporary library. Name what is
   missing, and when you substitute a gene-set source or an annotation build, say so
   beside the result, because that choice changes the numbers.
9. Say what did not reproduce, and why. When a published count cannot be matched, name
   the undefined choice (a threshold, a direction, a model) and compute the cheap
   alternatives beside your main one instead of tuning until it fits.
10. Report the state you actually reached. Say which outputs exist on disk, which cell
   was still running, and what a stopped turn left behind; the person continues from
   that record rather than from a claim that the work is done.
skills.intent: Run a whole analysis through the live sessions so a stop never loses the work.

skills.content:
Check how a page lays out in a real browser before you say it works.

Run `rho-screen-check <url or page.html>`. It opens the page at each viewport (by default 1440x900, 1024x768, 768x1024 and 390x844), waits for it to settle, writes one screenshot per viewport and prints a JSON report. Options: `--viewport WxH` (repeatable), `--out DIR` (default ./screen-check), `--overlap SELECTOR` (report the visible boxes of that selector that overlap one another), `--full-page`, `--settle MS` (default 800), `--browser auto|chrome|msedge|chromium|PATH` (default auto: Chrome, then Edge, then Playwright's Chromium).

Read the exit status first. 0: the check ran, and its findings are in the report. 1: an argument was wrong. 2: the check did not run; `error.kind`, `error.message` and `error.next` say why and what to do. Do what `next` says, then run it again.

For each viewport, read: `horizontalOverflow` with `scrollWidth` against `clientWidth` (the page is wider than the window); `elementsPastEdgeUnclipped` (what crosses the right edge and no box keeps in: read this count first), then `elementsPastEdge` (the first 50, unclipped first; `clippedBy` names the box that scrolls or hides what is beyond its own width); `unnamedButtons`; `overlaps` for your selector; `pageErrors` and `consoleErrors`; `httpErrors` (each response that failed, with its status and address); `requestsOutsideTarget` (what the page loads from elsewhere).

Then open each `screenshot` with the Read tool and say what you see. The report says what the page does, not whether a person can follow it; the screenshot and the flow answer that. Check the states a person reaches as well as the first screen: an empty state, an error, a long name or number, a narrow window, the screen after a step. Run the check again after each change.

Pitfalls seen in real runs:
- A selector can match hidden elements. The report counts visible boxes only; your own probes must filter by visibility too.
- The same attribute can appear in two views at once, such as a script editor's flow and a session's Data flow. Open a workspace that shows only the view you check.
- At 390 px the sidebar collapses and project labels are hidden. Reach the label through the page's own controls before you look for it.
- Text cut short inside a box of fixed height, such as a label that ends mid-word, is not in the report. Only the screenshot shows it.
- Restarting Rho ends the live R sessions, and the page then shows "Rho closed. Values defined before this are gone." Say so when a check follows a restart.
- Check a copy of the project, not the person's own project. A check must not change what the person has.
skills.intent: Check how a Rho screen or a local page lays out at phone and desktop widths, in a real browser, and read the result rather than assume it.

skills.content:
Edit a document buffer with a stable identity, explicit undo and conditional saves.
Use capability.list to discover the document operations this session may call.

1. document.open takes a project-relative path and returns the buffer with id, version
   and revision. Inside the project, never under .rho or .git: internal state is not
   an editable document.
2. Writes are conditional. document.edit takes expectedVersion and, when changeId is
   given, expectedRevision as well: the two travel together, always. A refused edit
   leaves the buffer and undo untouched; re-read and retry with the current numbers
   rather than replaying the old request under a new identity.
3. Undo has three distinct meanings. document.undoOwn reverses only the caller's own
   latest complete retained input group. document.revert reverses one named active
   change, possibly by another author, through targetChangeId. document.undo is the
   legacy global form and is not the human keyboard shortcut.
4. document.save writes disk only when the expected disk digest still matches. After
   a lost reply the save is pending: read the buffer to see pendingSave, and either
   resume the same request or abandon it with document.abandonSave, which never
   writes disk and keeps the buffer.
5. History is author-scoped. document.history lists retained entries;
   document.change.read returns exact before and after text for one change.

A browser tab may read and edit but never save: saving is an Agent or operator step.
Live editor bindings use {kind:"live-document",documentId}; a pinned binding keeps an
exact version and stays exact.
skills.intent: Edit a document buffer conditionally, with explicit undo and save conditions.

skills.content:
Keep resource identity and provenance explicit: bytes, a version, and where they came from.
Use capability.list to discover resource.list, resource.read, resource.register and artifact.check.

1. resource.register declares existing bytes with their kind and format, and requires
   expectedDigest of the current content. The returned {id, version} names those exact
   bytes; when the file changes, both change and old pages become stale on purpose.
Use resource.capture for immutable historical evidence: a project path or an exact Documents buffer version. A capture records observed bytes, not their producer or scientific validity.
2. resource.read is a bounded byte read with offset; resource.list reports retained
   resources with availability. Reads never start a runtime and never execute R.
3. artifact.check verifies the artifacts one run declared, against the completion
   inventory the producer wrote. Without a declared inventory there is nothing to
   check, and a missing inventory is not evidence of a missing artifact.
4. resource.list and artifact.check return registered references for declared run
   artifacts, including owner-state files. Bind those references directly to a view;
   resource.register remains limited to ordinary project files.

Declare a table key and namespace at registration if a later comparison or plot needs
entity identity; an unkeyed table stays readable but has no identity to compare on.
skills.intent: Register existing bytes with explicit identity, read them bounded, and verify produced artifacts.

skills.content:
Use native tools normally. Choose this managed R entry only when execution continuity
or a retained application operation is needed. It runs user-written R scripts, which
may invoke other native programs under existing permissions. Core is optional.
For a managed run, use capability.list to discover object.read, action.submit and
artifact.check in this session; reads address exported snapshots and execution is one
explicit submit that keeps its original operation identity.

1. Find the script. A disk script must match its declared digest; a buffer script is
   pinned by documentId and version. The bytes sent are the bytes in this request.
   If a body is not certain, protocol.validate { method, body } answers with the edit
   each problem needs before anything is sent.
2. Declare what the run produces, not what it might produce: artifacts carry path,
   kind and format, and their paths stay inside the run output directory.
3. The output directory exists before R starts and is handed to R as its first
   argument (commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)[1]). Write there directly; do not build
   the directory and do not use the working directory for outputs.
4. If you need artifact verification, declare completion: its filename is relative to
   the run directory, beside artifacts/, and the producer writes
   {"schemaVersion":1,"complete":true,"artifacts":[{"path","bytes","sha256"}]}.
   artifact.check reads that inventory; without it there is nothing to verify.
5. Read the outcome. A read of the operation reports the current outcome, so no
   separate observe is required: action.lookup and action.list reconcile a run that
   finished while nobody was watching. When the Host gives no answer the run stays
   active and the outcome is genuinely unknown; do not resubmit under a new identity.
6. A run belongs to whoever submitted it: only that session retries it. That session
   or the person, from a tab paired with this project, may stop it; cancellation.
   requestedBy names who asked, and a run the person stopped is not resubmitted unasked.
   Any session of this project reads a run by operationId (lookup, observe, output,
   artifact.check), so a run the person started from your proposed form is yours to
   follow. To repair a failed run, submit a new operationId with repairOf naming it.

An executed artifact lives under owner state (.rho/plugins/runs/...). It is verified
through artifact.check; it is not a project resource, so resource.register refuses it
and an Agent-run figure cannot be shown in a view. Do not claim it is presented.
skills.intent: Run an R script in this project and keep its produced artifacts.

skills.content:
Read and compare typed tables through stable resource identities.
Use capability.list to discover data.page, data.compare and resource.register.

1. Register the bytes first with resource.register and keep the returned {id, version}.
   A version names exact bytes: if the file changed, the version changes and the old
   pages become stale rather than silently mixing.
2. data.page takes offset and limit, an optional sort and an optional filter. It never
   addresses rows by position as identity: identity is the declared entity key, and an
   unkeyed table is readable but has none, so do not fabricate one.
3. data.compare joins two keyed tables and returns a new resource with provenance.
   The join is left, inner or full on declared key columns and namespaces.
4. Nulls stay nulls. A declared null value is not an empty string, and a comparison
   that finds no value on one side reports no value, not "absent from the file".

Reads are bounded observations: they never execute R and never change a resource.
skills.intent: Page and compare a typed table without inventing identity from row order.

failureRecipes.next: Register or re-read the current version; save the new {id, version} before paging again.

failureRecipes.message: Page size exceeds the configured limit.
failureRecipes.next: Ask for fewer rows; the earlier rows stay readable.

failureRecipes.message: Filter or sort names an unknown column.
failureRecipes.next: Use a declared column name from the registration, not a positional index.

failureRecipes.message: Compare needs two keyed tables in declared namespaces.
failureRecipes.next: Declare a key column and namespace at registration before comparing.

skills.content:
Plot two declared numeric columns from one immutable table version.
Use capability.list to discover data.plot.

1. Bind the exact {id, version} of a registered table. The plot reports the resource it
   read, so a chart never drifts from the bytes behind it.
2. Both coordinates must be declared numeric columns. The table must have an entity key
   and namespace, because each point carries its key.
3. A point budget downsamples with a deterministic stride; the reply says so and reports
   originalPoints, so a sparse chart is never mistaken for sparse data.
4. Plotting reads only. It runs no code and changes no resource; if the file changed, the
   version is stale instead of silently mixing two states.
skills.intent: Plot two numeric columns of one table version, bounded and reproducible.

failureRecipes.next: Register the table with a key column and namespace before plotting it.

failureRecipes.next: Name two columns declared as number; a string column cannot be a coordinate.

failureRecipes.next: Re-register the current bytes and plot the new version.

failureRecipes.next: Lower maxPoints or accept the deterministic downsample the reply reports.

skills.content:
Ask about a selected object and follow the answer without rebasing what was submitted.
Discover enabled operations with capability.list and skill.list.

1. An annotation anchors to an exact version: a UTF-16 document range or a stable table
   entity key at that resource version. A submitted message and its source snapshot stay
   exactly as submitted; a later edit does not silently move them.
2. annotation.create submits; annotation.read and annotation.list observe; annotation.reply
   answers and must name replyTo explicitly. Threads advance conditionally. Include
   resources: [{id, version}] for outputs that your reply refers to; these are explicit
   author links, not proof of scientific correctness. Preserve the original anchor.
3. To hand chosen feedback to an agent, build it with context.create and read it back
   through the tool with context.read. Prepared, read and explicitly replied are three
   different facts: reading is not understanding and not completion.
Human decisions are separate version-bound facts. Agents read them with annotation.read; only the authenticated person records annotation.decide. A later result never inherits an earlier decision.
4. Keep the original changeId after a lost acknowledgement and query the receipt boundary;

The Console records commands the person at this machine runs in the project folder.
Agents run their own commands with their own tools; an Agent may read this record with console.list and console.output.
The person may also keep terminals open here, each a shell in the project folder, and you may use them too. console.terminal.list lists them with who opened each. console.terminal.screen reads what one shows now as text. console.terminal.write types into it as if typed there: end a command with "\r". It returns the offset printed so far; pass it as after to console.terminal.screen with waitMs to wait until the output has come and stopped (quiet says it had). A full-screen program (an editor, top, less) has the screen while fullScreen is true; send its own keys, such as "q", to leave it.
Use a terminal for what the person has open or asks for there: a server they logged into, a program waiting for input, a command they want to watch. Work they need not watch is better done with your own tools. The person sees all that is typed and printed in a terminal, and your writes are recorded as your activity. A terminal whose shell is zsh, bash, fish, sh, dash or ksh93 (recording is true) records each command run in it with who typed it, the folder, the exit status and the start of what it printed; console.terminal.commands lists them, the newest first, so read the exit status there after the screen has settled. When a record is stored (more than its output was printed, or a full-screen program drew screens), console.terminal.output reads the rest in pages: the start and end that are kept, with a gap where the middle was not, and the last screens the program showed. console.terminal.open opens a terminal of your own, which the person can show beside theirs; wait for its prompt with console.terminal.screen (after 0, waitMs) before typing. You may close only the terminals you opened.
Use capability.list to see whether those reads are enabled for you.
A command keeps its changeId: repeating it returns the same record and never runs it twice.

A project has live R and Python sessions of its own, where your cells run unless you name a notebook, and each notebook the person opens in a workspace has its own R and Python sessions.
To look at data, check a value or try a model, run code with kernel.run (language "r" or "python") instead of a one-off Rscript -e or python3 -c: what you define stays in the session for the next cell, and the person sees each cell, its output, its plots and the variables.
Give each cell a short purpose. Pass waitMs to wait for it to finish; kernel.read reads it later.
To run a corrected version of an earlier cell, pass replaces with that cell's cellId: within the same session the notebook shows the new cell in its place, with the earlier run under it. After that session ends, the new run stands in its new session at its actual time; the old session keeps its cells. A cell that adds a step is a new cell.
A cell or session that kernel.read lists with a notebook belongs to that notebook; pass the same notebook to kernel.run (and kernel.inspect) to work there, and leave it out to work in the project's sessions. When the person asks for work in their notebook, the Notebook views of their workspace, with each one's notebook, are in the interface context of their message. Values made in one notebook are not in another.
A session starts with the first cell of its language in its notebook. Interrupt a cell that runs too long with kernel.interrupt; only the person stops a session.
Results meant to last still go to files from a script, so they can be rebuilt without the session. Run the script in the session (source("analysis.R"), exec(open("analysis.py").read())) rather than with Rscript or python3 from a shell: a figure file stays readable mark by mark only while it holds the bytes a cell saved.
A ggplot drawn in the R session (ggplot2 and what is built on it: ggtree, enrichplot, Seurat, patchwork) is also kept as a figure whose drawn marks are bound to the rows they come from; so is a page drawn with base graphics (bound where its points match a table in the session) and a ComplexHeatmap (each cell named by its row, column and value). The plot output names its layers and marks. Read it with figure.read {cellId, plot} to check what was actually drawn (marks per layer, rows missing, mappings) and to get the rows behind marks. A ggplot saved to a project file with ggsave() is kept as a figure of that file too: the cell names it under saved, and figure.read {path} reads it while the file keeps those bytes. When the person selects marks in a plot or a saved figure, their message names the selection.
Sessions can also run on a server. kernel.places lists the places and where each language runs; kernel.place.set names one (the server, its folder there, and setup lines run there before a session starts) or chooses it for R or Python; kernel.place.check connects and reports R and Python there.
kernel.servers lists the servers the person manages with serverctl and the skills bound to each: how that server is used (its environments, where heavy work goes, what to avoid there). Before you name a place on one or run code there, read the skills that apply with kernel.server.skill and follow them, for example in the place's setup lines. They guide the work on that server; they do not widen what you may do. A place on such a server is reached through serverctl, which holds its login; another server is reached with ssh.
The project's Python is the machine's python3 until you name another. When the work needs packages it lacks, make an environment in the project (python3 -m venv .venv or uv venv, then install into it) and pass interpreter: ".venv/bin/python" to kernel.run; later sessions of that language start with it too, and each cell records the program that ran it. A live session in which only you ran cells starts again with the program you name; once the person ran a cell in it, ask them to stop it first. Plots drawn in the project's live R session are kept as figures: every ggplot (ggplot2 and what is built on it, such as ggtree, enrichplot, Seurat and patchwork) is described after its cell, with each drawn point, bar, box, line or label bound to the built row it draws and, where the layer's statistic keeps its input rows, to the row of the plot's data. A page drawn with base graphics (plot, points, text, barplot, abline) is described from what it drew: each drawn part is a layer (points, text, rect, lines, abline) whose marks keep the values they were drawn at, in the data's units, and points or labels whose x and y are two columns of a table in the session (a data frame, a DataFrame, a matrix) are bound to its rows, directly or through -log10, log10, log2, log2(x + 1) or log1p; the layer's mapping names those columns (y: "-log10(padj)"), and its notes say how many marks were drawn elsewhere (clipped to the axis), or that an earlier layer of the plot draws the same column on the same axis through another transform, so the two layers place their marks on different scales. A ComplexHeatmap is described cell by cell: each cell names its row, column, value and slice, and its row of the matrix. A figure drawn with matplotlib in the live Python session (and what draws through it: seaborn, pandas .plot) is described from its artists: scatter points, line vertices, bars, heatmap cells (pcolormesh, seaborn heatmap and clustermap), segments, polygons and text labels are marks keeping the values they were drawn at; points, lines and labels whose x and y are two columns of a table in the session (a DataFrame, a Series, a 2-D array), directly or through -log10, log10, log2, log2(x + 1) or log1p, are bound to its rows, and the layer's mapping says which (y: "-log10(padj)"); a label drawn at a bound point names that point's row, or is bound by its text; a heatmap cell names its row, column and value, and its row of the session table drawn. A layer's notes say what the describer noticed: marks drawn elsewhere than their values, a column drawn on the same axis through another transform than an earlier layer of the plot draws it, or heatmap labels that name other rows than the values beside them; the cell's plot output carries them. A cell's plot output names its layers and marks when it was described, or figureProblem when it was not; other grid drawings and images (imshow) stay pictures. A ggplot the cell saved to a project file with ggsave(), a page drawn on a file the cell opened with png(), pdf() or svg() and closed with dev.off() (plotMA, a heatmap's draw(), a ggplot's print()), or a matplotlib figure saved with savefig(), is kept as a figure of that file too (the cell's saved list): name it by {path} instead of {cellId, plot} in both operations. It holds while the file keeps the bytes the cell saved; a file written again since is a picture.

1. figure.read {cellId, plot} returns the summary: each layer (counted from 0) with its geom, stat, mapping, constants, the data source its marks came from, how many marks it drew and whether they are bound to rows or groups (and why not); the plots, panels and facets; legend scales; and each source's columns and key column. Use it to check that a plot shows what you meant: the marks drawn against the source's rows, a mapping, a layer drawn from computed values.
2. Rows behind marks: pass marks ["L.M"] (layer L, built row M), selection (the person's selection named in their message), or where [{column, op, value}] with op eq, ne, lt, le, gt, ge, in or contains, on a source column or a built column (count, x). Each row gives the mark's built values and its source row with the key column (a gene, a cell barcode, a tree node).
3. To point the person at marks, figure.select {cellId, plot, marks, note, changeId}: they are shown highlighted in the plot with your note. It changes neither the plot nor its data; draw a new plot to change what is shown.

A mark is named only within its figure. Speak about the same things across figures by the source key (gene, barcode, ID). An R figure is drawn again from the plot object at 7 × 5 in, so labels placed at random (ggrepel) may sit slightly differently from the picture; a matplotlib figure is drawn at its own size. A selected mark is what was drawn; what it means is still for you and the person to establish.

Project skills are how work is done in this project: the methods the person chose, the conventions they keep and the traps its work ran into.
Each is a SKILL.md in the project's .claude/skills folder, read by the person and by every Agent here, in this conversation and later ones.
- Before you analyse, list the project's skills (skills.list) and read those whose description fits the task (skills.read). Follow them over your general practice, and say in your answer which you followed.
- Record in a project skill (skills.change) when the person corrects a method choice or says how they work, when you find the cause of a failure and the fix that works, or when you make a choice that changes results and the person accepts it.
- Record how to work, never results: no answers, values or data. Write each entry so it can be followed: what to do and when, in a line or two, with why if it is not obvious.
- Record a rule the person states in their terms and with their scope. Do not widen it, and do not fold another rule into its examples: an example that applies two rules at once becomes a third rule nobody stated.
- Keep one skill per method area, named for it, with a description saying when it applies. Keep it short: merge entries and drop those that no longer apply.
- Give each change a one-sentence reason and its evidence: the cell it came from (kind cell, its cellId), a file (kind file, its project path), or what the person said in their words (kind note). Use kind conversation only with the id of a Rho conversation.
- Read the skill first and pass its version as expectedVersion; a conflict means it changed, so read it again. A refused size means shorten it.
- A skill guides; it grants nothing and never widens what you may read, write or run. The person sees every change with who made it and why, and can undo it.

# Project notes

## When does the city need bikes?
<!-- rho:session c-91aa2e46b1ac1a6c -->

### Question

Compare the hourly demand profile on weekdays and weekends. Keep member and casual riders visible so a later question can use the same table.

### Data and method

- [data/rides/hourly_demand.csv](data/rides/hourly_demand.csv) contains twelve months of repeated weekday and weekend hourly observations.
- [analysis/hourly_demand.R](analysis/hourly_demand.R) aggregates the profile and writes `results/hourly_profile.csv` and `results/monthly_demand.csv`.

### Finding

Weekdays have morning and evening commute peaks. Weekend demand is lower overnight and broader through the middle of the day. See [results/hourly_demand.png](results/hourly_demand.png).

## Who rides at each time of day?
<!-- rho:session c-67f77cfebaba2cea -->

### Question

Summarize member and casual riders by day type and operating period. Identify where weather and season are likely to change the mix.

### Data and method

- The hourly table keeps temperature and rain beside the rider counts.
- [analysis/station_patterns.R](analysis/station_patterns.R) writes [results/rider_mix.csv](results/rider_mix.csv) and the stacked figure.

### Finding

Members dominate weekday commute periods. Casual riders make up more of the midday and weekend volume, which is where a simple temperature or rain sensitivity check would add the most value.

## Which stations need attention first?
<!-- rho:session c-fa24dfd80dfe4bcb -->

### Question

Use the station-by-hour table to find high-pressure stations, their peak hours and the first places to test a rebalancing rule.

### Data and method

- [data/stations/stations.csv](data/stations/stations.csv) holds the station context and capacity.
- [data/stations/station_hourly.csv](data/stations/station_hourly.csv) holds the hourly demand and utilization.
- [analysis/station_patterns.R](analysis/station_patterns.R) writes [results/station_demand.csv](results/station_demand.csv) and [results/station_heatmap.png](results/station_heatmap.png).

### Finding

Downtown and transit-hub stations have the largest commute peaks. Parks and the waterfront shift later into the day. Keep the station table beside the heatmap when deciding where a capacity change or rebalancing trial should start.

## Choices

- Used a compact, synthetic dataset so the example ships without a network download and every value can be inspected.
- Kept repeated observations across months and day types so the figures show seasonality and operating rhythm without pretending to be a city-wide census.
- Used rider type, station area and hour as the shared vocabulary across the tables, scripts and figures.

## To do

- [x] Build the hourly and station tables
- [x] Draw the three question figures
- [x] Put the conclusion in `results/summary.md`
- [ ] Add a real service-day feed and compare the fitted pattern with observed trips

Members dominate weekday commute periods. Casual riders make up more of the midday and weekend volume, which is where a simple temperature or rain sensitivity check would add the most value.

## Which stations need attention first?
<!-- rho:session c-fa24dfd80dfe4bcb -->

### Question

Use the station-by-hour table to find high-pressure stations, their peak hours and the first places to test a rebalancing rule.

### Data and method

- [data/stations/stations.csv](data/stations/stations.csv) holds the station context and capacity.
- [data/stations/station_hourly.csv](data/stations/station_hourly.csv) holds the hourly demand and utilization.
- [analysis/station_patterns.R](analysis/station_patterns.R) writes [results/station_demand.csv](results/station_demand.csv) and [results/station_heatmap.png](results/station_heatmap.png).

### Finding

Downtown and transit-hub stations have the largest commute peaks. Parks and the waterfront shift later into the day. Keep the station table beside the heatmap when deciding where a capacity change or rebalancing trial should start.

## Choices

- Used a compact, synthetic dataset so the example ships without a network download and every value can be inspected.
- Kept repeated observations across months and day types so the figures show seasonality and operating rhythm without pretending to be a city-wide census.
- Used rider type, station area and hour as the shared vocabulary across the tables, scripts and figures.
